description:
Frontera Signal | Tijuana, Mexico

We are a NASA Space Apps 2026 team combining software engineering, AI, Earth science and creativity. We transform NASA open data into scientifically grounded tools with real-world impact. Our focus: harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS observations to study historical wildfire patterns in Baja California and beyond. We seek collaborators in Python, GIS, data science, web development, UI/UX and communication. We value teamwork, rigor and open-source innovation.
summary:
We developed Frontera Signal, an interactive wildfire intelligence dashboard that integrates NASA FIRMS active fire detections (MODIS and VIIRS) with NASA POWER meteorological data across four Baja California border municipalities: Tijuana, Ensenada, Tecate, and Mexicali (2018–2026). Users explore regional hotspots on an interactive map and navigate a color-coded burning activity calendar to track monthly fire intensity, Fire Radiative Power, and historical percentiles. The platform lets users toggle between MODIS, VIIRS, and a harmonized multi-sensor view, compare sensor detections side-by-side via histograms, analyze local temperature, humidity, precipitation, and wind trends, inspect source-file evidence for data traceability, and export filtered datasets as CSV files.

Wildfires and agricultural burning across Northern Baja California threaten border communities, air quality, and ecosystems, yet relying on a single satellite sensor can undercount smaller or short-lived fires. By uniting multi-sensor NASA thermal observations with local climate drivers in an accessible, verifiable interface, Frontera Signal helps local responders, researchers, and residents identify shifting fire seasons and improve regional preparedness.
details:
Frontera Signal is an interactive wildfire intelligence dashboard that analyzes multi-year thermal anomalies and fire seasons across Baja California and four key border and coastal sub-regions (Tijuana & Playas de Rosarito, Tecate, Ensenada & San Quintín, and Mexicali & San Felipe) from 2020 to 2025.

Rather than merging incompatible satellite feeds, our Python scientific pipeline processes three independent NASA FIRMS active fire records (MODIS Terra/Aqua at 1,000 m, VIIRS Suomi NPP at 375 m, and VIIRS NOAA-20 at 375 m) alongside NASA POWER MERRA-2 monthly meteorological data. The web application organizes this data into four synchronized views:

  • Burning Calendar & Interactive Map: A multi-year monthly activity matrix colored by seasonal percentile, paired with a MapLibre GL JS map featuring four switchable basemaps (Dark, Satellite, Terrain, and Streets), regional/municipal filtering, and point-level inspection of Fire Radiative Power (FRP in MW), acquisition timestamp, day/night flag, and detection confidence.
  • Sensor Agreement Explorer: Quantifies how consistently MODIS and VIIRS capture the same seasonal trends by projecting detections onto a 10 km equal-area grid (EPSG:6933) and computing leave-one-out seasonal percentiles, Spearman rank correlation, and mean absolute percentile difference.
  • Environmental Context: Aligns monthly temperature (T2M), relative humidity (RH2M), bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), and wind speed (WS10M) with thermal activity to highlight hot, dry, and Santa Ana wind-driven fire regimes.
  • Evidence & Reproducibility: Exposes SHA-256 checksums, valid row counts, and collection versions for every ingested NASA source file, documents scientific limitations, and enables one-click filtered CSV exports.

Northern Baja California faces recurring chaparral wildfires, wildland–urban interface fires along the U.S.–Mexico border, and seasonal agricultural burning in the Mexicali Valley. However, raw fire pixel counts cannot be compared directly across satellites with different spatial resolutions (1,000 m vs. 375 m) and orbital overpass schedules.

Frontera Signal solves this translation gap by converting raw satellite detections into standardized, statistically comparable seasonal indicators. It equips municipal emergency planners, environmental researchers, cross-border air-quality monitors, and local residents with an accessible tool to distinguish genuine shifts in fire severity from sensor artifacts, pinpoint high-risk months by municipality, and export verifiable data for regional preparedness.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, & Software Used

  • NASA Data Resources: NASA FIRMS standard yearly archives (MOD14/MYD14 Collection 6.1, VNP14IMG Collection 2, VJ114IMG Collection 2) and NASA POWER monthly regional climate records (T2M, RH2M, PRECTOTCORR, WS10M).
  • Scientific Pipeline (Python): pandas, geopandas, shapely, pyproj, and numpy for spatial clipping, EASE-Grid 2.0 (EPSG:6933) 10 km grid aggregation, leave-one-out percentile calculations, and SHA-256 manifest generation.
  • Web Application (TypeScript): Next.js, React, MapLibre GL JS, ESRI basemap tiles, and custom responsive SVG charts.
  • Geospatial & Development Tools: geoBoundaries / INEGI 2020 administrative boundary data (MX-BCN), Git/GitHub for collaborative version control, and standard laptop workstations.

Most wildfire maps plot raw, uncalibrated hotspot dots that visually exaggerate modern 375 m VIIRS detections relative to historical 1,000 m MODIS records. Frontera Signal pairs strict sensor isolation with 10 km equal-area grid harmonization and leave-one-out seasonal percentiles, allowing users to compare sensors fairly at a glance. Combining a tactile multi-year Burning Calendar, four switchable geospatial basemaps, local meteorological anomalies, and cryptographic SHA-256 source provenance in a single zero-API-key interface bridges scientific rigor with immediate public usability.

Factors considered by our team:

  • Sensor Independence & Spatial Distortion: We enforced strict separation between MODIS and VIIRS scales and aggregated detections on an equal-area projection (EPSG:6933) rather than degree-based latitude/longitude grids.
  • Baseline Self-Inflation: When ranking how unusual a given month is, our pipeline compares it against the same calendar month across all other years in the 2020–2025 record so an extreme fire season does not distort its own reference baseline.
  • Non-Fire Thermal Anomalies & Sensor Limits: We explicitly documented agricultural burns, industrial heat sources, cloud obscuration, and orbital gaps in the Evidence tab so decision-makers understand what satellite thermal detections can and cannot confirm.
  • Zero-Friction Reproducibility: All pre-validated 2020–2025 GeoJSON and JSON outputs are bundled directly inside the repository so judges and community users can launch and inspect the full dashboard immediately without external API keys.
